summary:
Bangladesh's Penal Code of 1860, in Section 377, punishes "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" with imprisonment for life or a term of up to ten years and a fine. The explanation attached to the section treats penetration as sufficient and extends its ambit to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual acts. The provision was carried into Bangladesh's legal code at independence in 1971, and Parliament declined to repeal it in 2009 and again in 2013.

Whether Section 377 reaches sexual conduct between women is unresolved. A UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, dated September 2023 and updated April 2026, records the ambiguity: ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders.

Prosecutions are rare. Police use Section 377 instead to arrest, harass and extort people presumed to be LGBTIQ, including those read as effeminate, and the section has been invoked to restrict registration of LGBTI organisations. A suspicious-behaviour provision of the police code supplies a second basis for the same harassment.

Bangladesh officially recognises a third gender. A cabinet decision of 11 November 2013, chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, recognised hijra alongside male and female for identification on official documents; voter lists carry a third-gender option and in April 2019 "hijra" was introduced on voting forms so that people could vote under their proper gender identity. Gender-marker change is permitted. The recognition is narrow. No policy sets out what a person must undergo to change gender on official documents, no rule defines who qualifies as hijra, there is no protection against discrimination for hijra, and transgender people outside the hijra category remain unrecognised and unprotected.

The security position shifted with the August 2024 ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in the Monsoon Revolution. Global Press Journal reports that hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards and that trans lives have been upended, with its featured subject now living in hiding. A Washington Blade assessment of 5 August 2025 describes Bangladesh's LGBTQ community as increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats a year after the government fell.

JMBF's annual report, cited on 7 April 2026, documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across Bangladesh in 2025, described as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022. The violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. These are documented cases rather than a prevalence rate.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is documented within the past year. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district and known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025, with five unidentified individuals accused. No later killing is documented.

Police extortion drives violence against visibly trans people. After hijras refused to pay police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates in Narayanganj, a traditional livelihood. The policing reaches transit points. In April 2024 five transgender women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody.

State security forces have raided LGBTI gatherings. In May 2017 Rapid Action Battalion forces raided the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj during an LGBTI dinner, separated the 120 people present into small groups, beat them and arrested 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity, allowing media to photograph some detainees before later claiming the arrests were for narcotics possession; four were remanded, twelve held for questioning and twelve sent directly to jail. No later raid of this kind is documented.

Asylum-grade evidence records state-tolerated hostility. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 relied on country material recording Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Bangladeshi law recognises no same-sex relationship, civil union, domestic partnership or adoption route, and same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned and fined. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status enters that exposure directly.

Care access is constrained. The 2017 US Department of State report records social stigma against HIV and AIDS and against higher-risk populations as a barrier to health services, especially for the transgender community and men who have sex with men, and reporting documents hijra facing unequal access to housing and health care. Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated on 17 April 2022, in response to the US Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report, that treating LGBT rights and same-sex marriage as human rights is a regrettable and uncalled-for imposition of values from a select few countries.
tangentialFactors:
Formal inclusion and security decline run in parallel. Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013, a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021, hijra and LGBTIQ pride events have been held, and Outright International's country page updated 12 March 2026 records gender-marker change as allowed. The reporting covering the period after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution describes the opposite trajectory, with hardline conservative Islamist groups gaining ground and trans lives upended.

The 2017 US Department of State report characterises the transgender population as a long-marginalised but recognised part of society that faced continued high levels of fear, harassment and law-enforcement contact in the wake of violent extremist attacks against vulnerable communities. It records LGBTI members receiving threatening messages by telephone, text and social media, some harassed by police, and states that after the May 2017 raid and continued harassment many members including leadership reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, severely weakening advocacy and support networks. Organisations specifically assisting lesbians were rare.

The 2025 violation figure is a raw tally compiled by a national LGBTI rights organisation. The source gives no population denominator, so 260 documented violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals indicates direction of travel rather than comparative magnitude against other countries.

Foreign government reporting on LGBT issues has drawn an official rebuke. On 17 April 2022 Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the framing of the US Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report as an imposition of values, which bears on how much weight external monitoring carries domestically.
localsOnly:
Third-gender recognition is administered through the Ministry of Social Welfare, which counted approximately 10,000 hijra in a 2013 survey, most of whom were already enlisted as voters. In December 2014 the Ministry invited hijra to apply for government employment. In January 2015 the Ministry of Health issued a memorandum requesting the necessary steps to identify hijra by conducting thorough medical check-ups requiring them to strip and have their genitals confirmed, with photographs later released to confirm that they are "really men".

In July 2015, after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators, the government announced plans to recruit and enlist hijra as traffic police. A government housing scheme for homeless or landless individuals included transgender people for the first time, with at least 140 transgender community members provided government-built houses across the country. Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka, with classes starting 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects, free of charge and with no age limit.

Discrimination in employment and services is largely unaddressed. Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, caste or social status, and no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation exists. Hijra continue to face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care.

Education institutions have become sites of organised hostility toward trans presence. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam was excluded from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest, exam boycott and rally banners explicitly reading "no transgender". In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, a final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on stated grounds of online threats and carrying a weapon causing fear, which she denied, after she shared a satirical caricature. On 19 January 2024 part-time BRAC University lecturer Asif Mahtab Utsha publicly tore the seventh-grade History and Social Science textbook story "Sharifar Golpo", in which a character born male later identifies as a woman living as hijra, claiming it promoted homosexual and transgender concepts; student protests followed with "Say No To LGBTQ" banners and class boycott calls, and a five-member Education Ministry review four months later found nineteen words "incompatible" with Bangladeshi society and recommended their omission.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Section 377 reaches sexual conduct between women is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office note of September 2023, updated April 2026, records the ambiguity rather than settling it, and the two readings it cites contradict each other.

No source in this inventory sets out what a person must undergo to change gender on official documents in Bangladesh, nor defines who qualifies as a hijra. The recognition carried on official documents and voter lists therefore has no sourced procedure behind it.

Whether the January 2015 Ministry of Health verification memorandum remains in force is not sourced here, as is whether the government installed after August 2024 has altered any of these positions, including third-gender recognition or Section 377.

No source addresses entry or visa screening of trans travellers, document-marker treatment at Bangladeshi border points, or targeted inspection of trans arrivals. Nothing in this inventory supports a finding in either direction.

The 2025 violation count is a documented-case tally with no population denominator supplied, so it cannot be read as a rate or compared against other jurisdictions on magnitude.
